en: The preface to the *Recorded Sayings of the Four Houses of Huanglong* states:
"To speak all day long and yet find it insufficient is to exhaust the Way through speech. To speak all day long and yet find it sufficient is to exhaust phenomena through speech.
Both 'sufficiency' and 'insufficiency' fall into dualistic principles; how could the world ever recognize this? Now there was one, the fourth-generation descendant of Huanglong..."
Master Huiquan has personally transcribed the recorded sayings (*yulu*) of four masters—Jicui, Huītáng, Sīxīn, and Chāozōng—and requested that I write a preface for them.
As for these four great beings, they were the ones who brought radiance to the Chan school in the region west of the Great River. Some were said to be the reincarnations of Mazu;
some declined the master’s seat at Dàyuè; some responded to the thunder and lightning like an echo following a sound; and some [were as... six... [text fragment].

With roots of virtue superior and fervent, his true wind was indestructible and his reputation spread through the Way; the world looked up to him. At the mere touch of his sharp spiritual edge, ten thousand verses poured forth like water from one vessel to another.

Like a vast empty valley echoing every sound without remainder, or like a great round mirror reflecting every image without exception, he strung together pearls and wove patterns of precious shells that were scattered throughout the human realm.
In cloud-halls and moonlit windows, tens of thousands of mouths recited them; according to their respective capacities, whether small or great, all found within them something to sustain them.

To attain this teaching—can it truly be said that all things have been exhausted? Ultimately, both things and the Way are exhausted; it is simply for the listener to present themselves [to realization].
Within this, there is what is called "speaking all day long without ever having spoken," which moreover cannot be recorded by peeling skin or breaking bones.
That being so, is the Master Quan’s compilation of these questions and answers correct or not? To take it as...
It is thus: within the Vairocana-treasury there is a great scripture, yet its characters were never established from the beginning.

To regard this as "not so" is like a corpse dwelling while the dragon appears, or deep silence while the thunder roars; yet the sound and form have never been forgotten. Whether it be "this" or "not this," it remains ultimately undetermined.
Only when one understands this principle are both speech and non-speech equally True Suchness (*tathatā*). Without understanding this principle, [there is...]
To speak of "non-speaking" is likewise to fall into false views. From this, we know that the mind of Huìquán is the very mind of the Four Masters;

the insight of Huìquán is the very insight of the Four Masters. I shall arrange their teachings in order to show them to those who come after, thereby broadening the benevolence of the Four Masters in benefiting all beings.
Entering through sound, I do not begrudge my own person, so as to transmit the way of the Four Masters.
This is the grace [of the Buddha] and the original intent of the True Patriarch’s coming from the West. Those who would advance in this Way should attempt to evaluate it by means of this text.
Written on the fifth day of the third month in the eleventh year of the Xiangshu era. Preface by Qian Mi of Xiuzhou.
